Skin and Soft Tissue Infections MCB LE 3.03

Lecture Overview

Whole-lesson summary

  • Healthy and intact skin protects underlying tissues and provides excellent defense against invading pathogens.
  • Skin disease arises from three lines of attack: breach of intact skin, skin manifestation of systemic infection, and toxin-mediated skin damage.
  • The lecture then moves layer by layer and organism by organism:
    • Bacterial: Staphylococcal, Streptococcal, and other bacterial skin infections
    • Fungal: cutaneous and subcutaneous mycoses
    • Viral: mucocutaneous manifestations (warts, pox, herpes, exanthems, hemorrhagic fevers)

Framework: infection by skin layer

Folliculitis → Boils and carbuncles
↓
Dermis + dermal lymphatics
Erysipelas
↓
Subcutaneous fat
Cellulitis
↓
Fascia / below the dermis
Necrotizing fasciitis → gangrene or myonecrosis

I. Skin

A. Introduction

  • Healthy and intact skin (without any breaks) protects underlying tissues and provides excellent defense against invading pathogens.
  • The skin is colonized by an array of organisms which forms its normal flora.

Microbial load of normal skin is kept in check by:

FactorDetail
Limited moistureLimits the number of organisms
Prolonged exposure to moisture → increase in organisms
Moist areas (groin, armpit): organisms more numerous and more varied
Acidic pHLimits bacterial growth
Surface temperatureThere is an optimum temperature for the growth of microorganisms
Salty sweatHas lysozymes that can kill microorganisms
Excreted chemicalsSebum, fatty acids, and urea
Competition for nutrientsBetween invading species and normal flora

If organisms breach the stratum corneum, host defenses are mobilized:

Epidermal Langerhans cells elaborate cytokines
→
Neutrophils attracted to site of invasion
→
Complement activated via the alternative pathway

B. Microbial Lines of Attack on Skin

Line of attackDetails / Examples
1. Breach of intact skinInfection from the outside enters
Microscopic to major trauma
Accidental (laceration, burns) or intentional (post-surgery)
Hospitalized patients: pressure sores and intravenous catheter infections
2. Skin manifestation of systemic infectionBloodborne spread from infected focus to skin
Direct extension: draining sinuses from actinomycotic lesions, necrotizing and aerobic infection
3. Toxin-mediated skin damageMicrobial toxin produced at another site in the body
Rash in Scarlet Fever → erythrogenic toxin
Rash in desquamation of Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome

Classified based on skin layers and soft tissue involved.

II. Staphylococcal Skin Infections

Must KnowStaphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of skin infection and it provokes an intense inflammatory response.

A. Virulence Factors Table 1

Virulence factorFunction
Polysaccharide capsuleProtects from phagocytosis
Protein A, Clumping factor proteinsMediate adherence to host tissues
CatalaseNeutralizes peroxides produced by neutrophils and macrophages
CoagulaseConverts fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin clots that protect S. aureus from phagocytosis
Lipases, NucleasesCause tissue destruction
HyaluronidaseFacilitates the spread of infection
Exfoliative toxins A & BCause superficial layers of skin to peel off in scalded skin syndrome

B. General Presentation

  • Minor skin infections (boils or abscesses) and more serious post-operative wound infection.
  • Acquired from:
    • Self-inoculation from a carrier site (nose, inguinal region)
    • Contact with an exogenous source (another person)
  • Nasal carriers of virulent S. aureus may suffer from recurrent boils.
  • Serious skin disease due to toxin production: Scalded Skin Syndrome, Toxic Shock Syndrome.
  • CA-MRSA skin and soft tissue infections: of increasing incidence and concern.
    • Due to mecA gene → resistant to methicillin and penicillin

C. Furuncles and Carbuncles

Furuncles (boils) and carbuncles: large pus-filled nodules that can progress to deeper layers and spread into the blood.

Begins 2–4 days after inoculation in and around hair follicle = folliculitis
↓
Organisms multiply rapidly, spread locally → intense inflammation with influx of neutrophils
↓
Fibrin deposited → site walled off
↓
Abscess: abundant yellow, creamy pus (organisms + necrotic white cells)
↓
Expands slowly → erodes overlying skin → ruptures and drains

D. Staphylococcal Impetigo

  • Localized infection: pus-filled vesicles on an erythematous base followed by yellowish crust.
  • Mostly in children, on face and limbs.

E. Scalded Skin Syndrome

  • Localized infection with bacteria producing exfoliative toxins that spread through the blood → outermost layer of skin blisters and peels off.
  • Almost exclusively in very young children.

F. Diagnosis

  • Microscopy of gram-stained specimens is useful in pyogenic infections.
    • Not for food poisoning (intoxication)
    • Not for scalded skin syndrome and toxic shock syndrome (toxin-mediated)
  • Culture: on most laboratory media.
  • NAAT: sensitive, rapid detection of MSSA and MRSA.
TestSeparatesPositiveNegative
CatalaseStaphylococcus vs Streptococcus/EnterococcusStaphylococcusStreptococcus, Enterococcus
CoagulaseS. aureus vs other Staphylococcus spp.S. aureusOther Staphylococcus spp.
Agglutination (protein A)S. aureus vs other Staphylococcus spp.S. aureusOther Staphylococcus spp.

G. Treatment

  • Localized (abscess): incision and drainage (I&D).
  • Antibiotic therapy: indicated for systemic infections.
    • Empiric therapy should include antibiotics active against MRSA
  • Proper cleansing of wounds and antiseptics → help prevent infections.
  • Thorough hand washing and covering exposed skin → help medical personnel prevent spread.

III. Streptococcal Skin Infections

Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or group A beta-hemolytic Streptococci.

A. Diseases Caused

Suppurative (pus formation)Nonsuppurative (autoimmune, after strep pharyngitis)
Pharyngitis
Localized skin and soft tissue infections
Necrotizing fasciitis (flesh eating)
Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome		Rheumatic fever
Acute glomerulonephritis
High risk:
Children 5–15 years → pharyngitis
Children 2–5 years with poor personal hygiene → pyoderma

B. Virulence Factors Table 2

Virulence factorFunction
Outer hyaluronic acid capsuleProtects from phagocytosis
M proteins, M-like proteins, C5a peptidaseFound in the cell wall
Blocks complement-mediated phagocytosis
M protein also facilitates adherence and invasion into epithelial cells
Streptolysin S and OLyse erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets, cultured cells

C. Streptococcal Impetigo

  • Develops independently of streptococcal upper respiratory tract infection.
  • Acquired through contact with people with infected skin lesions. May colonize normal skin before invading through minor breaks.

Clinical features:

  • Acute, develop within 24–48 hrs of skin invasion → marked inflammatory response.
  • Also called pyoderma or impetigo contagiosa. Most often affects young children.
  • Caused by S. aureus and GAS.
  • Papules → pustules → crusty lesions. Crusts typically golden or honey colored.
  • Cutaneous cuts or abrasions increase risk.

Transmission:

  • Contact with someone with impetigo is the most common risk factor (including drainage).
  • Poor personal hygiene increases risk.
  • More common in summer (temperate) and in tropical/subtropical locations.
  • Lesions on exposed areas: mostly face and extremities.

Diagnosis: lab testing not necessary nor routine. Gram stain or culture of exudate/pus can identify cause.

Treatment: oral and topical antibiotics covering both Staphylococcus and Streptococcus.

D. Scarlet Fever (Scarlatina)

  • Some strains produce streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin (formerly erythrogenic toxin).
  • SPE A, B, and C act on skin and blood vessels → diffuse erythematous rash, may occur with strep pharyngitis.
  • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: especially associated with speA.
  • Anyone can get it. Age and close contact increase risk.

Clinical features

  • Scarlatiniform rash with GAS infection (pharyngitis, wound infection).
  • Erythematous rash that blanches on pressure with sandpaper-like quality.
  • Pastia's lines: accentuation of red rash in flexor creases.
  • Begins on trunk, spreads outwards, usually spares palms and soles.
  • Persists about 1 week → desquamation may follow.
  • Yellowish white coating with red papillae on tongue → disappearance → strawberry tongue.

Diagnosis

  • RADT or throat culture. RADT: high specificity, varying sensitivity vs culture.
Must Know ❗Throat culture is the gold standard diagnostic test.

Treatment: antibiotics shorten symptoms, reduce transmission to close contacts, prevent complications.

E. Cellulitis

  • Infection in the subcutaneous tissues caused by multiple bacteria. Most common cause: S. pyogenes.
  • Clinical: erythema, pain, warmth. Poorly demarcated. May have fever and chills.
  • Diagnosis: usually clinical. Cultures might help in animal bites, immersion injuries, immunocompromised.
  • Treatment: oral antibiotics for mild. IV for systemic infections.

F. Erysipelas

  • Involves the upper dermis, extends into superficial cutaneous lymphatics.
  • Tender, intensely erythematous indurated plaque with a sharply well demarcated border.
    • Well-defined margin differentiates it from cellulitis
  • Usually face and legs.
Key Differentiator — 3 distinguishing features Lesions are raised above surrounding skin.
Clear demarcation between involved and uninvolved tissue.
Lesions are a brilliant salmon red.

Diagnosis: high WBC, raised CRP, positive blood culture.
Treatment: amoxicillin, clavulanic acid, cephalexin, cloxacillin.

G. Necrotizing Fasciitis

  • Rapidly progressive infection that destroys deep soft tissues.
  • Isolation of S. pyogenes with or without others. S. aureus = most common co-infecting species.
  • Strains with M protein types 1, 3, 12, and 28 typically produce pyrogenic exotoxin A.
  • Immunocompromising conditions increase risk.
  • Most commonly extremities, particularly legs. Heat, erythema, swelling, tenderness.

Quick progression

Swelling
→
Brawny edema
→
Dark red induration (dermal papilla vessels thrombosed)
→
Red → purple → blue → black (gangrene)
→
Skin anesthetized (superficial nerves die)

Diagnosis: Gram stain (GAS vs other organism).
Treatment: early and aggressive surgical exploration with debridement + broad spectrum parenteral antibiotics.

IV. Other Bacterial Skin Infections

A. Anaerobic Cellulitis / Gas Gangrene

  • Develops in traumatized or devitalized tissues, surgical or traumatic wounds, ischemic extremities.
  • Diabetic patients are prone.
  • Gas gangrene / clostridial myonecrosis → Clostridium perfringens.
    • Organism and spores in soil and human/animal feces → enter traumatized tissue
  • Foul smelling discharge, marked swelling, gas in the tissues.
  • Areas with poor blood supply: buttocks and perineum (ischemic vascular disease, peripheral arterial sclerosis).
  • Characteristic: clostridia invade deeper into the muscle.
  • Alpha toxin hydrolyzes lipids in cell membrane → cell lysis and death.

Diagnosis: mixture of organisms cultured from wound.

Exam TrapAntibiotics are adjuncts to surgical debridement, not a replacement.

B. Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes

Puberty: increased responsiveness to androgenic hormones
↓
↑ Sebum production, ↑ keratinization, ↑ desquamation in pilosebaceous ducts
↓
Blocked ducts become sacs → C. acnes and normal flora (Micrococci, yeasts, Staphylococci) multiply
↓
Acts on sebum → fatty acids and peptides + enzymes from bacteria and polymorphs → inflammation

Treatment: Tetracyclines.

C. Mycobacterium leprae (Hansen's disease)

  • Transmission: overcrowding, poor hygiene. Via direct contact and aerosol inhalation.
    • Few organisms shed from skin lesions
    • Nasal secretions of lepromatous patients are laden with M. leprae
  • Not highly contagious: prolonged exposure needed. Children living with an open case are most at risk.
  • Incubation may be many years. Onset is gradual.
  • Grows intracellularly in: skin histiocytes, endothelial cells, Schwann cells of peripheral nerves.
  • Spectrum depends on presence or absence of cell mediated immune response.
  • Acid fast rods in nasal scrapings and lesion biopsies.
Tuberculoid leprosyLepromatous leprosy
SkinBlotchy red lesions with anesthetic areas on face, trunk, extremitiesExtensive skin involvement, large numbers of bacteria
OtherPalpable thickening of peripheral nerves (organisms multiply in nerve sheaths)Loss of eyebrows, thickened nostrils, ears, cheeks → leonine facies
Progressive destruction of nasal septum
PrognosisBetter—
TreatmentDapsone + Rifampicin for 6 monthsDapsone + Rifampicin + Clofazimine for 1–2 years

V. Fungal Infections of the Skin

A. Cutaneous Mycoses

  • Among the most common infections in humans.
  • Superficial (Pityriasis versicolor, Tinea nigra, Black and White piedra): mainly cosmetic problems.
  • Cutaneous (ringworm / tineas by dermatophytes): more significant.

Malassezia furfur — Pityriasis / Tinea versicolor

  • Malassezia (Pityrosporum) furfur: common skin inhabitant.
  • Commensal → pathogen: phase change from yeast to hyphal forms.
  • Promoting factors: hot humid weather, excessive sweating, oily skin, weakened immunity, hormonal changes.
  • Also involved in seborrheic dermatitis and dandruff.
  • Clinical: trunk and proximal limbs. Hypo- or hyperpigmented macules coalescing into scaling plaques. Not usually itchy. Some resolve spontaneously.
Clinical Cue10% KOH scrapings: short hyphae and yeast cells = "spaghetti and meatballs".

Treatment: topical azole (ketoconazole, clotrimazole) OR Selenium sulfide 2.5% lotion.

Dermatophytes

Transmission and pathogenesis

  • Spread through arthrospores (thick-walled vegetative cells from hyphae).
  • Direct contact with skin, from soil, animals, or other humans.
  • Anthropophilic species are the most common cause.
  • Produce proteases (break down keratin) and kinases/pseudokinases (modulate host metabolism).
  • Ability to attach to keratinized tissues = basis of dermatophytosis.

Causative agents

  • Genera: Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum.
  • T. rubrum: most common species (80–90% of strains). Also T. mentagrophytes, M. audouinii.
  • Zoophilic (temperate countries): T. verrucosum (cattle), T. mentagrophytes (rodents), M. canis (cats and dogs).
  • T. tonsurans: most common cause of tinea capitis.

Clinical presentation

  • Itchy, balding, red rash. Circular/ovoid lesions with sharp elevated edges (may have vesicles).
  • Advance centrifugally, leaving central clearing and mild scaling → "ringworm".
  • Skin dry and scaly. Hair infection → hair loss.
  • Dermatophytid reaction: hypersensitivity from circulating fungal antigens (erythema or vesicles).
  • Cracked, macerated skin → superinfection.
TineaBody part
CapitisHair and skin of scalp
CorporisBody
CrurisCrotch
ManuumHands
UnguiumNails
PedisFeet

Diagnosis

  • 10% KOH: septate, branching long narrow hyphae.
  • Most fluoresce under UV light → aid for tinea capitis.
  • Culture on Sabouraud's agar.
Hair infectionArthrosporesOrganism
EctothrixOUTSIDE the hair shaftMicrosporum spp.
EndothrixWITHIN the hair shaftMajority of Trichophyton

Treatment

  • Localized tinea corporis: topical (clotrimazole, ketoconazole) once or twice daily for 2–3 weeks.
  • Systemic oral antifungals: required for scalp, more effective for nails.
  • Terbinafine or Itraconazole now preferred over Griseofulvin.

Candida Skin Infections

  • Opportunistic. Most commonly secondary infection in immunocompromised.
  • Common inhabitants of oral cavity, GIT, vagina, penis. C. albicans colonizes oropharyngeal, esophageal, GI mucosa.
  • Requires moisture: dryness limits growth. Rapidly colonizes damaged skin and intertriginous sites.
  • Intertrigo: inflammatory dermatosis of opposing skin surfaces.
    • Pain and itching → high morbidity
    • Predisposing: obesity, DM, immunosuppression
    • Treatment: topical nystatin and azoles
  • Untreated → systemic infection, may lead to sepsis.

B. Subcutaneous Mycoses — Sporotrichosis

  • Subcutaneous fungal infections are rare.
  • Sporothrix schenckii: saprophytic dimorphic fungus in soil, on roses, barberry bushes.
  • Acquired through trauma (thorn prick, insect bite). Occupational hazard: farmers, gardeners, florists.
  • Papule/nodule at trauma site → secondary nodules along the lymphatic tract.
  • Diagnosis: culture on Sabouraud's agar.
  • Treatment: Amphotericin B (induction) → Itraconazole.

Mycetoma

  • Chronic progressive subcutaneous infection: tumor-like swellings with sinuses discharging grains with sulfur.
  • Most commonly the foot = "Madura foot". Also hands.
  • After trauma. Farmers and people without footwear.
  • Diagnosis: biopsy for histopathology + bacterial and fungal culture. PCR identifies, but culture is essential for susceptibility testing.
TypeAgentTreatment
ActinomycetomaBacteria: Nocardia brasiliensis, Actinomyces israeliiAntibiotics (Cotrimoxazole)
EumycetomaFungi: Madurella mycetomatisSurgical debridement + prolonged antifungal

VI. Skin Manifestations of Viral Infections (A–D)

Rashes

  • Particular features of human infection: skin is naked and highly reactive, immune and inflammatory events clearly visible.
  • Cause discomfort, may be painful, and help diagnosis.

A. Papillomaviruses (HPV)

  • Icosahedral, dsDNA. Cause skin papillomas or warts.
  • Transmission: direct contact, also indirectly via floors and fomites.
Enters via surface abrasions
→
Infects basal layer cells
→
Cells stimulated to divide
→
1–6 months: visible papilloma/wart

Wart forms

  • Filiform: finger-like projections
  • Flat-topped: grow inwards (plantar warts)
  • Cauliflower-like: genital warts
  • Flat area of dysplasia: cervix

Associated with cancer of cervix, vulva, penis, rectum, head and neck (oropharyngeal).

HPV typeDisease
6 and 11Anogenital warts (sexually transmitted)
16 and 18Cervical cancer
1 and 4Plantar warts and cutaneous lesions
2, 3, and 10Warts on knees and fingers

Diagnosis: HPV DNA detection (type and viral load).
Treatment: karyolytic agent salicylic acid. Destruction by cryotherapy (dry ice, solid CO2, liquid nitrogen). Liquid nitrogen: commonly used and most effective.

B. Poxvirus — Molluscum Contagiosum

  • Umbilicated lesion caused by a Poxvirus. Infects epidermal cells → fleshy lesion with umbilicated centers.
  • Spread by contact, genital lesions by sexual intercourse, infected objects.
  • Round, firm, painless umbilicated bumps. Scratching spreads to nearby skin.
  • More common in children, also immunocompromised adults. Immunocompetent adults: via sexual activity.

Smallpox (Variola)

Must Know ❗First human infectious disease to be successfully eradicated worldwide.
  • Clinical concern: potential for release and weaponization.
  • dsDNA, Orthopox genus, Poxviridae family.
  • Transmission: airborne respiratory droplets, direct contact with lesions or fomites.
  • Viral particles released from sloughing oropharyngeal lesions → aerosolization.
  • Febrile prodrome (high fever, chills, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, back ache) → skin lesions 1–3 days later.
  • Begin on forearms or face → rest of body. Lesions at the same stage throughout.
Macules
→
Papules
→
Vesicles
→
Pustules
→
Crusts

Tecovirimat: first antiviral for smallpox. Vaccination: led to global eradication.

C. Herpes Simplex Virus

  • dsDNA, Herpes virus group.
HSV-1HSV-2
LesionsOropharyngealGenital herpes
TransmissionKissing (saliva, cold sores)Sexual intercourse

HSV-2 arose as a sexually transmitted variant of HSV-1, but sites infected are now less clearly distinct.

  • Painful vesicles. Latent in sensory ganglia for life.
  • Reactivation with fever or stress → spreads down sensory nerves → lesions at original site.
  • Primary infection sites: mouth/lips/gingiva (recurrent ulcers), eye (conjunctivitis, keratitis), fingers (herpetic whitlow), rubbing/trauma (herpes gladiatorum, wrestlers), genital tract (HSV-2).
  • Diagnosis: PCR for HSV DNA in vesicular fluid.
  • Treatment: Acyclovir (systemic or topical), Valacyclovir, Famciclovir.

D. Varicella-Zoster Virus

  • Primary → varicella (chickenpox). Reactivation → herpes zoster (shingles).
  • Transmission: respiratory secretions, vesicle fluid (contact or aerosol).
  • Latent in sensory dorsal root ganglia. Infection → lifetime immunity.

Varicella / Chickenpox

  • Prodromal fever and malaise 1–2 days before rash.
  • Lesions first on scalp, face, trunk: red macules → fluid-filled vesicles. Intensely pruritic.
  • Appear in clusters and crops → different stages of development.
  • Infectious: 48 hours before rash until all lesions dried completely.
  • Predominant complication: secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus, S. pyogenes), particularly children.
  • Varicella pneumonia: more severe in smokers and chronic lung disease.
  • Others: hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, purpuric hemorrhagic rash, arthritis, myocarditis, pericarditis, nephritis, acute retinal necrosis.
Oral acyclovir: proven benefit only if given in the first 24 hours.
Prophylaxis with oral acyclovir if no VzIg: start 7–10 days post exposure, for 7 days.
VzIg: for those without immunity at high risk of severe varicella after significant exposure.

Herpes Zoster / Shingles

  • When cell-mediated immunity declines → reactivation. Most common in elderly or immunocompromised.
Must Know ❗Pain: first symptom, occurring in the dermatome where the lesions subsequently arise.
Limited to a single dermatome without crossing the midline.
Thoracic and lumbar dermatomes more frequent.
Ramsay Hunt syndromeOphthalmic Zoster
Peripheral facial nerve palsy with vesicles in the ear or mouthOcular manifestations, sight threatening
Oral acyclovir recommended in:
Immunocompetent hosts if lesions < 72 hours old
All immunocompromised patients with shingles
ZostaVax (US): reduces shingles in adults 60–70 years, decreases risk of post herpetic neuralgia.

VI. Skin Manifestations of Viral Infections (E–I)

E. HHV-6 & HHV-7 — Roseola Infantum

  • Double-stranded, enveloped. Transmission: respiratory secretions.
VirusDisease
HHV-6ADeterioration of HIV to full-blown AIDS
HHV-6BMajority of clinical disease: Roseola Infantum / 6th Disease / Exanthem Subitum
HHV-7Mostly asymptomatic. Small proportion of roseola in older children (~3 years)
  • Self-limiting febrile illness in infants 4 months to 2 years.
  • Acute high grade fever lasting 3 days. Also irritability, coryza, GI upset.
  • Resolution of fever heralds the rash: rose-pink, blanching, non-pruritic rash on trunk or face.
  • HHV-6B: most common cause of febrile convulsions.
  • HHV-6 encephalitis likely from reactivation. Frequently detected post transplant.

F. Parvovirus B19

  • Tropic to erythroid progenitor cells. Transmission: respiratory droplets.
  • Febrile illness in children with facial rash = "Slapped Cheek Syndrome" → Erythema infectiosum / 5th disease.
  • Grows in bone marrow → temporary fall in hemoglobin.
    • Serious in chronic anemia or sickle cell anemia → aplastic crisis
  • Can cause arthralgia in adults.
  • Diagnosis: serology for B19 IgM. Molecular tests for B19 DNA in fetal blood when hydrops fetalis suspected.
  • No antivirals available.

G. Rubeola / Measles

  • Single stranded negative sense, helical, enveloped RNA virus. Worldwide.
Must Know ❗Humans: only reservoir.
  • Airborne and contact via respiratory droplets. Infects upper respiratory tract and conjunctiva. Droplets airborne up to 2 hours.
  • Highly contagious. 2–4 day prodrome: malaise, high fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis.
  • Infectious during prodrome until 4 days after rash.
Must Know ❗Koplik spots are pathognomonic white papules on an erythematous base affecting the buccal mucosa, seen during this phase.
  • Exanthem around day 3–4 with high fever.
Behind the ears
→
Face
→
Trunk
→
Limbs (palms/soles may be involved)
→
Fever drops on reaching soles

Rash: erythematous, maculopapular, confluent as disease progresses.

Complications

  • Opportunistic bacterial: otitis media, pneumonia (virus damages respiratory surfaces).
  • Giant cell pneumonia: primary measles pneumonia in cell-mediated immune defects.
  • Post-infectious encephalitis. SSPE: 1 to 10 years after apparent recovery.
  • Worse in poor-care/malnourished children due to: poor mucosal defenses (improved by Vit. A), protein-calorie malnutrition + virus-induced immunosuppression, poor antibiotic access.

SiteWell-nourished, good careMalnourished, poor care
LungMild respiratory illnessLife-threatening pneumonia

Must Know ❗Routine childhood vaccination: key strategy to reduce measles deaths (95% vaccine efficacy).
Vaccines contain live-attenuated strains, usually as MMR or MMRV.
MMR two-dose: 12–15 months, then 4–6 years (school entry).

H. Rubella / German Measles

  • Single stranded positive sense, enveloped, icosahedral RNA.
  • Mild febrile childhood illness, but infection in pregnancy → major fetal risk.
  • Transmission: person-to-person droplet.
  • Prodrome: mild malaise, mild conjunctivitis, tender posterior auricular lymphadenopathy, fever.
  • Maculopapular rash concurrently or 1–5 days after onset, resolves in 3–4 days.
  • Rash: forehead → face → trunk and limbs (rapid).
  • Infectious 7 days before to 7 days after rash. Shedding maximal when rash is erupting.
  • Many are asymptomatic or without rash but still transmit.
Warning — Congenital Rubella SyndromeMother acquires virus during pregnancy → significant congenital morbidity and mortality.
First trimester infection has major consequences.
Miscarriage, stillbirth, premature labor, severe birth defects.

I. Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers

  • Hemorrhagic rashes: severe and invariably fatal spectrum of VHF disease.
  • VHF: several families of enveloped RNA viruses, tied to specific animal hosts or vectors → restricted geography.

Cram Sheet

❗ Must-Know Points Throat culture is the gold standard diagnostic test (scarlet fever with pharyngitis).
Smallpox: first human infectious disease successfully eradicated worldwide.
Zoster: pain is the first symptom in the dermatome where lesions arise.
Measles: humans are the only reservoir.
Koplik spots: pathognomonic white papules on erythematous base, buccal mucosa.
Routine childhood vaccination: key measles strategy (95% efficacy, MMR at 12–15 mo and 4–6 y).
Chikungunya hallmark: fever, arthralgia, rash.

Skin basics

  • Load controlled by: limited moisture, acidic pH, temperature, salty sweat (lysozyme), sebum/fatty acids/urea, competition.
  • Breach → Langerhans cytokines → neutrophils → complement (alternative pathway).
  • 3 lines of attack: breach, systemic (blood or direct extension), toxin-mediated (scarlet fever, staph TSS).

Staph aureus

  • Most common cause of skin infection. Nasal carriers → recurrent boils.
  • CA-MRSA → mecA.
  • Coagulase: fibrinogen → fibrin. Hyaluronidase: spread. Exfoliative A & B: scalded skin.
  • Gram stain not useful for toxin-mediated disease (food poisoning, SSS, TSS).
  • Catalase + (Staph) → Coagulase + / Protein A + (S. aureus).
  • Abscess → I&D. Systemic → antibiotics, empiric MRSA coverage.

Strep pyogenes

  • Nonsuppurative: rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis.
  • Pyoderma risk: 2–5 y with poor hygiene. Pharyngitis: 5–15 y.
  • M protein: blocks complement-mediated phagocytosis, adherence.
  • Impetigo: papule → pustule → honey crust, independent of URTI.
  • Scarlet fever: SPE A, B, C. speA → strep TSS. Sandpaper, blanching, Pastia's lines, spares palms/soles, strawberry tongue.
  • Erysipelas: raised, demarcated, salmon red. Cellulitis: poorly demarcated.
  • Nec fasc: M types 1, 3, 12, 28 (exotoxin A). S. aureus = common co-infection. Primary Rx: surgery.

Other bacteria

  • C. perfringens: gas gangrene, alpha toxin (lipid hydrolysis), diabetics, buttocks/perineum.
  • C. acnes: androgens → sebum → blocked sacs → fatty acids → inflammation. Rx tetracyclines.
  • M. leprae: Schwann cells, acid fast, nasal secretions. Tuberculoid (better, D+R 6 mo) vs Lepromatous (leonine, D+R+C 1–2 y).

Fungi

  • Tinea versicolor: yeast → hyphal change, hypo/hyperpigmented, spaghetti and meatballs.
  • Dermatophytes: arthrospores, keratin. T. rubrum (80–90%), T. tonsurans (capitis), M. canis (cats/dogs).
  • Ringworm: central clearing. Dermatophytid = hypersensitivity.
  • Terbinafine/itraconazole preferred over griseofulvin.
  • Sporotrichosis: rose thorn, nodules along lymphatics, Ampho B → itraconazole.
  • Mycetoma: Madura foot, sinuses with grains. Actino → cotrimoxazole. Eumyco → surgery.

Viruses

  • Molluscum: umbilicated, painless, poxvirus.
  • Smallpox: macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → crust, same stage. Tecovirimat.
  • HSV: latent in sensory ganglia. Whitlow, gladiatorum. PCR. Acyclovir.
  • VZV: latent in dorsal root ganglia. Infectious 48 h before rash until crusted. Ramsay Hunt (facial palsy + ear vesicles) vs ophthalmic (sight threatening).
  • Roseola: 3-day fever → rash. HHV-6B → febrile convulsions. HHV-6A → HIV to AIDS.
  • Parvo B19: erythroid progenitors → aplastic crisis in sickle cell. Adults: arthralgia. No antivirals.
  • Measles: prodrome cough, coryza, conjunctivitis. SSPE 1–10 y later. Vit A helps mucosa.
  • Rubella: infectious 7 d before to 7 d after rash. First trimester → CRS.
  • Dengue: 4 serotypes, cross-protection < 6 months, white areas of sparing.
